answers.question: A funny anecdote about Benjamin Franklin.
answers.answer: Benjamin Franklin was known for his humor and wit [d02-0371]. In Congress, when it was suggested that the Episcopal clergy should stop praying for the king, Franklin joked that the clergy had been praying for the king's wisdom for twenty years without any effect, making the measure unnecessary [d02-0371]. He also wrote humorous pieces, such as a reply to the claim that American sheep had little wool, where he joked that the tails of American sheep were so laden with wool they needed little wagons to keep them off the ground [d01-0214]. Additionally, Franklin admitted to creating amusing anecdotes and fables to fill newspaper columns when news was scarce, such as the story of Polly Baker, which he made up to entertain readers [d04-0625].

Benjamin Franklin was born on January 6, 1706, old style (January 17, 1706, new style), in Boston, Massachusetts, in a house on Milk Street opposite the Old South Church, on the morning of a Sabbath day [d01-0021, d02-0018]. His father, Josiah Franklin, had emigrated from Banbury, England, and was an intelligent and industrious man guided by high moral and religious principles; he worked as a tallow-chandler and soap-boiler, and Benjamin assisted him in this trade until about twelve years old [d02-0016, d01-0023, d06-0011]. Benjamin's mother was from the Folger family, from whom he inherited humane and liberal traits [d01-0022]. He grew up in a large family with sixteen siblings, including brothers James, John, Peter, and Josiah, and sisters Lydia and Anne Harris [d02-0028, d04-0540, d04-0546].

Benjamin's father initially intended him for the church and sent him to grammar school at age eight, where he quickly became a top student, but his formal education was cut short due to the family's limited means [d01-0022, d06-0008]. After attending a school for writing and arithmetic, he left at ten to help his father in the tallow-chandler business, which he disliked [d06-0009]. At about eleven, he was apprenticed to his brother James in the printing business for nine years, reluctantly accepting this path [d02-0028]. During his apprenticeship, Franklin devoted himself assiduously to learning the printing trade, often sacrificing leisure and sleep [d02-0030]. He continued his education through self-study and extensive reading while working as an apprentice [d06-0008, d02-0030, d05-0860].

Franklin's first job was helping his father in the tallow-chandler business, cutting wicks, running errands, and tending the shop [d06-0009, d02-0028]. He briefly tried the cutler's trade but abandoned it due to apprenticeship terms [d02-0028]. Later, he apprenticed with his brother James as a printer, which he pursued for three years [d02-0028, d02-0030]. At age twenty, Franklin secretly escaped his apprenticeship by boarding a vessel to New York at night, using a false story to conceal his departure; his passage was swift and pleasant [d02-0056, d02-0111]. He then embarked on a long voyage to Philadelphia aboard the ship Berkshire, which took eighty days, keeping a diary filled with witty and wise remarks during the journey [d02-0111].

In his youth, Franklin made a serious mistake when he took advantage of a woman's company and attempted liberties which she repulsed, causing a breach with his friend Ralph that lasted thirty-five years [d02-0106]. He also faced difficulties during his apprenticeship when a political piece he wrote offended the Assembly, leading to his brother's imprisonment for refusing to reveal Franklin as the author [d06-0023]. Around age twenty-one, Franklin suffered from pleurisy, a serious illness that nearly killed him [d05-0103].

Franklin had six children with Deborah, including Francis Folger, who died at about four years old, and Sarah Franklin [d02-0017, d04-0469, d02-0267]. Sarah had seven children, including Benjamin Franklin Bache and Richard Bache [d04-0516].

Franklin lived primarily in Philadelphia after moving from Boston, frequently visiting New York, and spent about twenty-six years living in England and France combined [d04-0014, d04-0018]. Early in 1777, he took up residence at Passy in France, where he remained during his stay in the country [d02-0421, d06-0171]. He also traveled to Scotland, Ireland, and other Continental countries during his life [d04-0018].

Among Franklin's inventions was the Franklin stove, also called the Pennsylvania fireplace, designed for better warming of rooms while saving fuel [d01-0069]. He also completed the musical instrument called the harmonica [d03-0437] and discovered the identity of lightning and electricity using simple materials [d05-0735]. Franklin was known for his ingenuity in local improvements, such as getting pavements laid, organizing street sweeping and lighting, and he valued the habit of integrity, which helped him gain influence despite being a poor speaker [d01-0078, d04-0053].

Franklin was known for his humor and wit, often using jokes and humorous writings to entertain and make points, such as his witty remarks in Congress and amusing newspaper anecdotes [d02-0371, d01-0214, d04-0625]. He had close friends throughout his life, including early companions John Collins, Joseph Watson, Charles Osborne, and James Ralph, and later intimate friends such as Mary "Polly" Stevenson, Mrs. Paschal, Thomas Mifflin, William Hunter, Jean Holker and his wife, John Joseph Monthieu, Turgot, Doctor Benjamin Rush, Charles Carroll of Carrollton, and Samuel Chase [d02-0087, d04-0736, d04-1062, d04-0633, d04-0630].

One of the hardest experiences Franklin endured was a severe and cruel journey to Montreal in the spring of 1776, which was very taxing for a man of his age and nearly cost him his life due to fatigue and exposure [d01-0323]. He also narrowly escaped shipwreck off Falmouth Harbor on his second voyage to England and faced dangerous conditions when arriving in a deserted New York expected to be bombarded [d04-0198, d02-0384].

Benjamin Franklin died on April 17, 1790, after suffering chest pain and difficulty breathing; his last known words were "A dying man can do nothing easy" [d01-0622, d04-0654]. His funeral was attended by a great procession and many citizens, and Congress voted to wear mourning for one month [d01-0622]. He is remembered with great respect and tributes from many groups, having risen from humble beginnings to high station, wealth, and distinction through prudence and honesty [d01-0622, d04-0654, d06-0174].

Early in 1777, he took up residence at Passy in France, where he remained during his stay in the country [d02-0421, d06-0171].
He also traveled to Scotland, Ireland, and other Continental countries during his life [d04-0018].
Among Franklin's inventions was the Franklin stove, also called the Pennsylvania fireplace, designed for better warming of rooms while saving fuel [d01-0069].
He also completed the musical instrument called the harmonica [d03-0437] and discovered the identity of lightning and electricity using simple materials [d05-0735].

Franklin was known for his ingenuity in local improvements, such as getting pavements laid, organizing street sweeping and lighting, and he valued the habit of integrity, which helped him gain influence despite being a poor speaker [d01-0078, d04-0053].

Franklin was known for his humor and wit, often using jokes and humorous writings to entertain and make points, such as his witty remarks in Congress and amusing newspaper anecdotes [d02-0371, d01-0214, d04-0625].

He had close friends throughout his life, including early companions John Collins, Joseph Watson, Charles Osborne, and James Ralph, and later intimate friends such as Mary "Polly" Stevenson, Mrs. Paschal, Thomas Mifflin, William Hunter, Jean Holker and his wife, John Joseph Monthieu, Turgot, Doctor Benjamin Rush, Charles Carroll of Carrollton, and Samuel Chase [d02-0087, d04-0736, d04-1062, d04-0633, d04-0630].

Franklin faced rivals and enemies, including Lee and Izard, and political opponents such as Dr. William Smith and the Proprietary Party in Pennsylvania, who directed many attacks against him [d04-0665, d04-0666, d05-0266].

checks.sentence: One of the hardest experiences Franklin endured was a severe and cruel journey to Montreal in the spring of 1776, which was very taxing for a man of his age and nearly cost him his life due to fatigue and exposure [d01-0323].

He also narrowly escaped shipwreck off Falmouth Harbor on his second voyage to England and faced dangerous conditions when arriving in a deserted New York expected to be bombarded [d04-0198, d02-0384].
Benjamin Franklin died on April 17, 1790, after suffering chest pain and difficulty breathing; his last known words were "A dying man can do nothing easy" [d01-0622, d04-0654].
His funeral was attended by a great procession and many citizens, and Congress voted to wear mourning for one month [d01-0622].

He is remembered with great respect and tributes from many groups, having risen from humble beginnings to high station, wealth, and distinction through prudence and honesty [d01-0622, d04-0654, d06-0174].
